sentences.text: Bicentenaria was a small bipedal predator with an estimated body length of 2.5 to 3 meters.
This animal weighed approximately 40 kilograms.
The anterior upper jaw teeth possessed serrations only at the base of the tooth crown.
The praemaxilla bone carried at least four teeth that had a circular cross-section.
Most teeth lacked serrations, with the exception of one tooth featuring serrations on the upper half of its anterior margin.
Fossil evidence indicates the creature possessed claws that were strongly curved and flattened transversely.
The hand claws on the outer fingers displayed tops with posteriorly overhanging edges.
Lips and lumps on the posterior edges of some claws served as attachment points for muscles used in stretching and flexing.
The only known maxillary tooth was very flattened and showed striations on both cutting and exiting edges extending to the tip.
The quadratum bone was robust, lacked pneumatization, and contained a small, high-placed foramen quadraticum.
The quadratojugal bone featured a frontal branch twice as long as its ascending branch.
The longest known sacrum consisted of four fused vertebrae, though researchers believe the total count was likely five.
Despite its small size, this bipedal predator reached lengths between 2.5 and 3 meters and weighed about 40 kilograms.
Its uniquely curved and flattened claws bore specific structural features like lips and lumps for muscle attachment.
The teeth showed unusual patterns, with serrations restricted to specific parts of the crown rather than the entire edge.
Bones and claws were discovered in 1998 by Rauel Spedale and friends after a drop in water levels at the Ezequiel Ramos Mexía Reservoir exposed fossils.
The find occurred near Lago Ramos Mejía in Río Negro Province, Argentina, by Raúl Spedale, a concrete company employee who was fishing.
A local school teacher recognized the uniqueness of the find and contacted paleontologist Raúl Ortiz.
Between 1999 and 2000, Spedale used a hammer and chisel to remove a thirty to forty centimeter surface layer at a depth of half a meter to expose more bones.
Further excavation became impossible after the water level in the lake rose again.
The discoverer initially believed the fossils belonged to a machairodontine cat.
The holotype specimen MPCA 865 consists of the back of a skull attached to the back of the lower jaws.
The species Bicentenaria argentina was formally described and published by Novas et al. in August 2012.
The name was first published in press articles in June 2012 and formally described in an article in August 2012.
Because multiple specimens, including a juvenile, were found together, researchers concluded that Bicentenaria lived in groups.
The parent group for Bicentenaria is Coelurosauria.
Bicentenaria is classified in the class Reptilia.
Novas et al. (2012) classified Bicentenaria within Coelurosauria, determining it to be less basal than Tugulusaurus.
The describers placed Bicentenaria in a very basal position within Coelurosauria.
According to a cladistic analysis, it is phylogenetically close to Tugulusaurus but just below the Tyrannosauroidea, which are in turn more basal than Compsognathidae.
It is likely the first representative of a new basal Coelurosauria lineage, phylogenetically close to Tugulusaurus.
The type species of the genus Bicentenaria is B. argentina.
The genus Bicentenaria was described by Novas et al. in 2012.
Bicentenaria was described by Novas et al. in 2012.
Bicentenaria lived during the Early Cretaceous (Albian) period in the Candeleros Formation of Argentina.
The fossils were found in Candeleros Formation layers dating to the Cenomanian, approximately 95 million years ago.
Bicentenaria lived during the Late Cretaceous period.
Bicentenaria lived approximately 90 million years ago during the Turonian stage of the Late Cretaceous in what is now South America.
The time range for the genus is the Albian stage, from 113.2 to 110.1 million years ago.
